state.misconception_label: Thinks alternate angles are always equal

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are arguing about alternate angles. Tom says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are alternate. Katie says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are equal. Who is correct? ![Shows two non parallel lines that are intersected by another line. Angles P and Q are both on the outside of the lines and on opposite sides of the transversal.](). I got Only
Katie because I assumed all the angles in the figure are equal.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Tom is actually correct in this scenario. Alternate angles are not always equal; they are only equal when the lines being intersected are parallel. Can you think of a way to determine if angles \( p \) and \( q \) are equal in this case?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, I think I get it a bit better now. So, if the lines aren't parallel, then the alternate angles can be different, right? But how do I know if the lines are parallel or not just by looking at the angles?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: That's correct! To determine if the lines are parallel, you can look for special angle relationships such as corresponding angles or alternate interior angles. Can you identify any other angle pairs on the diagram that might help us determine if the lines are parallel?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher directly addresses the misconception that alternate angles are always equal by clarifying they're only equal when lines are parallel, and the student shows partial understanding by Turn 2, though the final question about identifying angle pairs suggests incomplete resolution of the original misconception.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher uses questioning to guide discovery rather than directly explaining the concept with worked examples, which is inconsistent with the traditional strategy of explicit instruction and demonstration.
